title: Job 33:19–33
context: Job 33:19–33 completes Elihu’s first speech. He describes a person chastened with pain on his bed, wasting away until he draws near to the pit (33:19–22; compare Proverbs 3:11–12). Then he says, “If there is beside him an angel, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to show to man what is right for him,” God is gracious and says, “Deliver him from going down to the pit, I have found a ransom.” (33:23–24). The word rendered angel can also mean messenger, and readers take the figure as a heavenly angel, as a human messenger or teacher (some suggest Elihu presents himself in that role), or as a mediator-figure; the text does not say what the ransom is, and readers suggest the person’s repentance, the messenger’s intercession, or a provision from God himself. Psalm 49:7–8 and 49:15 also speak of a ransom and of redemption from the power of Sheol. Elihu’s messenger may be read alongside Job’s wish for an umpire (9:33), his witness in heaven (16:19–21), and his Redeemer (19:25); these passages are named without being harmonized, and readers differ on how they relate. Christian readers in both traditions have commonly heard in 33:23–24 a later pointer to Christ (compare 1 Timothy 2:5; Mark 10:45); this is a common later reading, not the only sense of the passage, and not a point of contrast here. Questions about the scope of Christ’s ransom are treated in the existing boxes at Mark 10:45 and 1 Timothy 2:5. The restored person prays, sees God’s face with joy, confesses his sin, and praises God for redemption from the pit (33:25–28; compare 2 Kings 5:14; Psalm 30:3; Psalm 56:13). Elihu says God does these things two or three times with a person (33:29–30), and he ends by inviting Job to answer, “for I desire to justify you” (33:32), or else to listen (33:31–33).

verses.text: “He is chastened also with pain on his bed, with continual strife in his bones,
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says a person “is chastened also with pain on his bed, with continual strife in his bones”. Arminian readers note that Elihu presents suffering as a possible form of God’s discipline, and they compare Proverbs 3:11–12, named here without harmonizing, while cautioning against applying this to every case.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu introduces pain as a second way God speaks, a theme Eliphaz also touched on (5:17), though Elihu develops it at greater length. They read the idea of corrective suffering as shared ground, while noting that the prologue gives a different reason for Job’s afflictions.

verses.text: so that his life abhors bread, and his soul dainty food.
verses.arminianNotes: The sufferer’s life abhors bread and his soul dainty food. Arminian readers note the realistic description of illness that takes away appetite, and they see Elihu describing a condition close to Job’s own, which makes his account of God’s purposes in pain pointed and personal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the description of loss of appetite fits severe illness. They read the verse as part of Elihu’s portrait of suffering that brings a person low, and they observe that the details resemble Job’s own laments about his condition (compare 6:7).

verses.text: His flesh is so consumed away that it can’t be seen. His bones that were not seen stick out.
verses.arminianNotes: The sufferer’s flesh is consumed so that it cannot be seen, and his bones stick out. Arminian readers note the vivid picture of wasting away, and they observe that Job has described his own body in similar terms (compare 19:20), which makes Elihu’s description apply closely to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same resemblance to Job’s laments. They read the verse as stressing how near to death a person can come under God’s discipline, and they observe that Elihu describes this as a stage in a process that can end in restoration.

verses.text: Yes, his soul draws near to the pit, and his life to the destroyers.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “Yes, his soul draws near to the pit, and his life to the destroyers.” Arminian readers note that the destroyers may be powers or messengers of death, though the exact sense is uncertain, and they see the verse as marking the low point before deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the pit and the destroyers picture the threat of death, and they hold the identification of the destroyers loosely. They read the verse as setting the scene for the intervention of the messenger in the following verse.

verses.text: “If there is beside him an angel, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to show to man what is right for him,
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu speaks of “an angel, an interpreter, one among a thousand”. Arminian readers note that the word rendered angel can also mean messenger, and they hold open whether a heavenly being, a human teacher, or a mediator-figure is meant, naming Job 9:33, 16:19–21, and 19:25 without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identity open. They note that Christian readers in both traditions have commonly heard here a later pointer to Christ (compare 1 Timothy 2:5), and they label this a common later reading, not the only sense of the verse and not a point of contrast.

verses.text: then God is gracious to him, and says, ‘Deliver him from going down to the pit, I have found a ransom.’
verses.arminianNotes: God is gracious and says, “Deliver him from going down to the pit, I have found a ransom.” Arminian readers note that the text does not say what the ransom is, and they hold open whether it is the person’s repentance, the messenger’s intercession, or a provision from God himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identity of the ransom open, and they name Psalm 49:7–8 and 49:15. They note the common later Christian reading that connects it with Mark 10:45, and they leave questions about the scope of Christ’s ransom to the existing box at Mark 10:45.

verses.text: His flesh will be fresher than a child’s. He returns to the days of his youth.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “His flesh will be fresher than a child’s. He returns to the days of his youth.” Arminian readers note the picture of complete restoration, and they compare Naaman, whose “flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child” (2 Kings 5:14), named here without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same comparison and read the verse as describing God’s power to restore what suffering has wasted. They observe that Job’s own restoration at the end of the book (42:10) comes in a different way from the one Elihu describes.

verses.text: He prays to God, and he is favorable to him, so that he sees his face with joy. He restores to man his righteousness.
verses.arminianNotes: He prays to God, who is favorable to him, so that he sees God’s face with joy, and God restores to man his righteousness. Arminian readers note the restored relationship with God, and they emphasize the person’s prayer as a real response to God’s gracious initiative.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse places restoration within God’s favor and gift, and they read the phrase restores to man his righteousness as God’s act of renewal. Both traditions see shared ground here in God’s gracious welcome of a person who turns to him.

verses.text: He sings before men, and says, ‘I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it didn’t profit me.
verses.arminianNotes: The restored person sings and says, “I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it didn’t profit me.” Arminian readers note the public confession of sin, and they compare Psalm 32:5, named here without harmonizing, as another place where confession leads to praise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same parallel and the honesty of a confession that admits sin brought no gain. They read the verse as shared ground about repentance, while observing that Elihu’s account assumes a sinner’s restoration, which the prologue does not say of Job’s case.

verses.text: He has redeemed my soul from going into the pit. My life will see the light.’
verses.arminianNotes: The restored person says, “He has redeemed my soul from going into the pit. My life will see the light.” Arminian readers note the praise of God’s redemption from death, and they compare Psalm 30:3 and Psalm 103:4, named without harmonizing, as similar songs of deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same parallels and read the verse as the climax of Elihu’s description: God redeems from the pit and gives life. They treat this as shared ground for both traditions, without pressing it into a later doctrinal framework.

verses.text: “Behold, God does all these things, twice, yes three times, with a man,
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “Behold, God does all these things, twice, yes three times, with a man”. Arminian readers note that God’s warnings and disciplines are repeated, and they see in this God’s patience in calling people back more than once before they reach destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same patience and read the repetition as part of God’s persistent care for those he disciplines. They hold this as shared ground, while noting that Elihu does not say how many chances a person has, and the verse should not be pressed into a rule.

verses.text: to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of the living.
verses.arminianNotes: God acts to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of the living. Arminian readers note the phrase the light of the living, also found in Psalm 56:13, and they see God’s purpose in discipline as bringing a person back to life and joy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same phrase and read the verse as stating God’s restorative purpose clearly. They observe that both traditions share this hope, and they note that Elihu here summarizes his account of how God speaks through dreams and pain.

verses.text: Mark well, Job, and listen to me. Hold your peace, and I will speak.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “Mark well, Job, and listen to me. Hold your peace, and I will speak.” Arminian readers note that Elihu again calls for Job’s attention, and they observe that he asks Job to be silent even as he has earlier invited Job to answer him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the alternation between inviting Job to speak and asking him to listen. They read it as Elihu’s eagerness to complete his argument, and they observe that readers differ on whether it gives Job real room to respond.

verses.text: If you have anything to say, answer me. Speak, for I desire to justify you.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “If you have anything to say, answer me. Speak, for I desire to justify you.” Arminian readers note Elihu’s stated desire to see Job vindicated, and they see in it a hopeful motive that sets him apart, at least in intention, from the three friends.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu’s wish to justify Job may mean to see him in the right or to see him restored. They read the verse as showing that Elihu’s aim is Job’s good, while observing that the book leaves the evaluation of his speech to the reader.

verses.text: If not, listen to me. Hold your peace, and I will teach you wisdom.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu ends, “If not, listen to me. Hold your peace, and I will teach you wisdom.” Arminian readers note that Elihu presents himself as a teacher of wisdom, and they leave it to readers to weigh his claim in light of the LORD’s speeches that follow later in the book.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu’s offer to teach wisdom closes his first speech confidently. They observe that the book does not comment on his speeches when the LORD speaks, and they hold that how Elihu’s teaching relates to the LORD’s answer is debated.
